title: The Flight of the Nez Perce
intro: In 1877 several non-treaty bands of the Nez Perce refused to give up their ancestral lands and move to a reservation in Idaho Territory. Led by a coalition that included Ollokot, White Bird, Toohoolhoolzote, Looking Glass and Chief Joseph, they fought a retreat of 1,170 miles (1,880 km) while pursued by the United States Army, first to seek help from the Crow and then to reach Sitting Bull's camp in Canada.
ending: The war ended at the Bear's Paw Mountains, 40 miles (64 km) from the border, where 418 Nez Perce surrendered and were sent to Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. White Bird escaped with an undetermined number of his band to Sitting Bull's camp in Canada.

legs.title: From the homeland to the Clearwater country

stops.text: After General Howard ordered the non-treaty bands onto the reservation within 30 days, Joseph and the other leaders judged resistance futile. They agreed to the move and reported to Fort Lapwai as ordered.
stops.quote: The other Nez Perce leaders, including  Chief Joseph, considered military resistance to be futile; they agreed to the move and reported as ordered to Fort Lapwai, Idaho Territory.

stops.text: At White Bird's camp at Tolo Lake, three young men set out on a mission of revenge for the earlier killing of a relative by a white man. They killed four white men and wounded another, and about sixteen more young men then rode out to raid the settlements.
stops.quote: Thus humiliated and apparently fortified with liquor, Shore Crossing and two of his cousins, Sarpsisilpilp (Red Moccasin Top) and Wetyemtmas Wahyakt (Swan Necklace), set out for the Salmon River settlements on a mission of revenge. On the following evening, June 14, 1877, Swan Necklace returned to the lake to announce that the trio had killed four white men and wounded another man.

stops.text: The bands camped in the canyon and decided to avoid war but fight if forced. Cavalry under Captain Perry approached, and after shots were fired at a truce party the Nez Perce routed them, killing 34 soldiers while three Nez Perce warriors were wounded.
stops.quote: By June 16, the bands had moved to the southern end of White Bird Canyon, about five miles (8 km) long, one mile (1.6 km) wide at its maximum, and bounded by steep mountain ridges.

stops.text: After crossing and recrossing the Salmon River, the warriors rebuffed the army in a series of skirmishes near Cottonwood.
stops.quote: After crossing and recrossing the Salmon River, the warriors rebuffed the army in a series of skirmishes near Cottonwood, Idaho, July 3–5, 1877.

stops.text: After Howard's force attacked their Clearwater camp, about 250 warriors and 500 women and children, with more than 2,000 horses and other livestock, crossed from Idaho over Lolo Pass into Montana Territory.
stops.quote: They crossed from Idaho over Lolo Pass into Montana Territory.

stops.text: Forces tried to halt the Nez Perce at a barricade here, but the Nez Perce bypassed it.
stops.quote: Forces attempted to halt the Nez Perce at Fort Fizzle, but the Nez Perce simply bypassed the barricade.

stops.text: The two-day battle in southwestern Montana Territory left heavy casualties on both sides, including many Nez Perce women and children. Afterwards the war grew fiercer, and the Crow refused the Nez Perce refuge, so they decided to try to reach Canada.
stops.quote: The most notable was the two-day Battle of the Big Hole in southwestern Montana territory, a battle with heavy casualties on both sides, including many women and children on the Nez Perce side.

stops.text: While Howard's men were camped at Camas Meadows, the Nez Perce raided at night and stole horses and mules. They held off the cavalry that pursued them and continued into Yellowstone National Park.
stops.quote: With Howard's men camped at Camas Meadows, the Nez Perce conducted a nighttime raid in the early hours of August 20 and stole horses and mules.

stops.text: The Nez Perce travelled along what was later named Nez Perce Creek across the Central Plateau and Hayden Valley. They crossed the Yellowstone River at Nez Perce Ford and left by a difficult route across the Absaroka Mountains.
stops.quote: The Nez Perce fled through Yellowstone, travelling along what was later named Nez Perce Creek across the Central Plateau and Hayden Valley, crossing the Yellowstone River at Nez Perce Ford and exiting via a difficult route across the Absaroka Mountains.

stops.text: The army caught up with them in the canyon of Canyon Creek, west of Billings. The warriors took positions in the hills and fought a delaying action before escaping over the hills.
stops.quote: The army next caught up with the Nez Perce on September 13 in the canyon of Canyon Creek, west of Billings.

legs.title: The Bear's Paw Mountains and exile

stops.text: The Nez Perce camped on the prairie beside Snake Creek, only 40 miles from the border, believing they had shaken off their pursuers. General Miles's force made a surprise attack on the camp in the morning.
stops.quote: The war came to an end when the Nez Perce stopped to make camp and rest on the prairie adjacent to Snake Creek in the foothills of the north slope of the Bear's Paw Mountains in Montana Territory, only 40 miles (64 km) from the Canada–United States border.

stops.text: After a three-day standoff Howard arrived on 3 October. Chief Joseph surrendered on 5 October, saying he would fight no more forever. White Bird escaped with an undetermined number of his band to Sitting Bull's camp in Canada.
stops.quote: The war ended after a final five-day battle fought alongside Snake Creek at the base of Montana's Bears Paw Mountains only 40 miles (64 km) from the Canada–US border.

stops.text: Miles marched his captives 265 miles (426 km) to the Tongue River Cantonment in southeast Montana Territory, where they were held until 31 October.
stops.quote: Miles marched his captives 265 miles (426 km) to the Tongue River Cantonment in southeast Montana Territory, where they arrived on October 23, 1877, and were held until Oct. 31.

stops.text: The able-bodied warriors were marched to Fort Buford. On 1 November the women, children, the ill and the wounded set out for it in fourteen Mackinaw boats.
stops.quote: On November 1, women, children, the ill and the wounded set out for Fort Buford in fourteen Mackinaw boats.

stops.text: Most of Bismarck's citizens turned out to welcome the prisoners with a buffet. On 23 November they were loaded into eleven rail coaches for the journey to Fort Leavenworth.
stops.quote: A majority of Bismarck's citizens turned out to welcome the Nez Perce prisoners, providing a lavish buffet for them and their troop escort.  On November 23, the Nez Perce prisoners had their lodges and equipment loaded into freight cars and themselves into eleven rail coaches for the trip via train to Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.

stops.text: Over the protests of the fort's commander, the Nez Perce were forced to live in a swampy bottomland. Howard and Miles had promised a return to Idaho, but General Sherman overruled them.
stops.quote: Over the protests to Sherman by the commander of the Fort, the Nez Perce were forced to live in a swampy bottomland.

stops.text: After Joseph pleaded in Washington in January 1879, the government refused to let the Nez Perce return to Idaho because of fierce opposition there. They were sent to Oklahoma and settled on a small reservation near Tonkawa.
stops.quote: Instead, Joseph and the Nez Perce were sent to Oklahoma and eventually located on a small reservation near Tonkawa, Oklahoma.

stops.text: Joseph and 268 surviving Nez Perce were allowed to return to the Pacific Northwest. Joseph was not permitted to go back to the Nez Perce reservation and settled at Colville, where he died in 1904.
stops.quote: In 1885, Joseph and 268 surviving Nez Perce were finally allowed to return to the Pacific Northwest.  Joseph, however, was not permitted to return to the Nez Perce reservation but instead settled at the Colville Indian Reservation in Washington.

notes: Clearwater left out as a stop: the article gives only 'the valley of the Clearwater River' and no place or date. Wallowa homeland left out (a valley/region). No Canada stop: article places Sitting Bull's camp nowhere. Doubtful wp titles: 'White Bird, Idaho' (town near the canyon), 'Camas Meadows' (may redirect to the battle), 'Canyon Creek, Montana', 'Bear Paw Battlefield', 'Fort Keogh' (article names only the Tongue River Cantonment), 'Yellowstone National Park' (a large area). Big Hole's article mentions no killing of women and children by name beyond 'heavy casualties ... many women and children on the Nez Perce side'. Tolo Lake date uses the 14 June evening report; ceremony was 13 June. 1877 is the article's year for all June-October dates. Bismarck stop: article places the Fort Abraham Lincoln route 8-10 November; train loading date given for Bismarck citizens' welcome context. places.tsv has no match (big-hole is not checked as same place; entry left null). Fort Buford date is the departure from Tongue River, not arrival.
